newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia opens roads in Kalimantan after riots.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia opens roads in Kalimantan after riots.

text.p: The Indonesian military has opened several roads into the interior of West Kalimantan as peace gradually returns to the riot-hit province, a military officer said on Friday.

"The roads heading to areas such as Sanggau have been reopened. We have lifted the curfew as the situation gradually returns to normal," the officer told Reuters by telephone from Pontianak, the coastal capital of West Kalimantan on Borneo island.
He declined to give other details, but said: "People here are healing their wounds after all the disturbances." Overnight curfews had been imposed in Pontianak and other centres.

The official Antara news agency quoted army chief of staff General Raden Hartono as saying on Friday many people had become victims of the riots between the native Dayak and Moslem migrants from Madura island off eastern Java since late December.
"The victims are many. There is more than one civilian, but there is only one security officer (among the victims)," he said. Antara gave no further details.
The local military and residents in the province say at least 12 people have died over the past six weeks. Some residents and church sources say the figure could be much higher.

Trouble erupted in the province bordering Malaysia's Sarawak state in what police said was a fight between Dayak and Maduran youths over a girl at a concert in Sanggau Ledo, about 95 km (60 miles) north of Pontianak.
The fighting spread to other parts of the province. In Sanggau, 140 km (90 miles) east of Pontianak, Maduran families have taken refuge in army camps after a series of fights between the two groups.

The Merdeka newspaper quoted Major-General Namuri Anoem, head of the Tanjungpura military command that oversees Kalimantan's four provinces, as saying on Thursday 68 people had been arrested for their involvement in the riots.
He said the suspects, who were being questioned at the local police headquarters, came from both ethnic groups.
The London-based Tapol human rights group said at least 17 Dayaks had been killed at a military roadblock early this month. Military officials were not available to comment on the report.
Diplomatic sources said it appeared that in some cases, soldiers had fired in self-defence.
Most Dayaks are Christian while the Maduran migrants are Moslem, like most Indonesians. At least 19 people have died in religious and ethnic riots in Indonesia since October.
